title: 📖 10 — Campaign Rules & Play Systems
rawNotionMarkup: Edition II continuity and provenance note. The preceding edition's complete accessible chapter is carried forward rather than summarised. This chapter remains subject to future creator revisions and the pending ChatGPT-export comparison. ## Supreme creative principle — RULE OF COOL ALWAYS PREVAILS Creator clarification, 21 November 2026: The Rule of Cool takes precedence over pedantic realism. This is an adventurous fantasy world, so something impressive, imaginative or spectacular can happen even if it would be highly implausible in our world. The comparison to Warhammer 40K Orks was humorous shorthand for that spirit—not an instruction to make reality obey belief or to give everyone automatic success. After trying the strongest possible reading, the creator specifically said “Not quite to that scale though lol.” Final creator clarification — appearance is NOT a feasibility test: In Eryndor, “just because it looks ridiculous doesn't mean it won't work; it doesn't mean it will, either.” An absurd-looking weapon, rickety machine, eccentric plan, fantastical construction or seemingly impossible stunt gets a fair chance on its own merits. Neither a bonus for looking cool nor a penalty for looking silly. Its actual function or outcome depends on the relevant in-world capability, workmanship, circumstances, experience, preparation, resistance and sometimes luck, allowing fantasy to transcend ordinary Earth expectations. Rule of Cool means imaginative possibilities are genuinely permitted—not automatically successful. Practical GM instruction: Don't reject a proposal because a realist says “that would never work,” and don't award success just because it's spectacular. If it works in this world, allow it, even if observers think it ludicrous. If it fails, the failure should have a credible in-world cause, not ridicule of the idea. Let surprises go both ways: a laughable contraption might excel and an imposing masterpiece might collapse. Preserve uncertainty, player agency, danger and meaningful consequences. The Warhammer 40K Orks reference was a joking analogy about unexpected effectiveness, not imported belief-based reality-warping mechanics. What real history is for: Inspire grounded social texture and conflicts—farming, markets, laws, labor, slavery, trade, guilds, governance, armies, hospitals, beliefs, festivals and everyday life. Don't impose medieval demographic limits or scientific ceilings on established populations, geography, gravity, moons, magic or wondrous fantasy devices. Karak-Varn is 22.8 million in the current adopted model (3.8 million was an old baseline) and all source-established peoples and scale are preserved. Examples: A dwarf may conceive an audacious rune-powered machine or survive a daring combat maneuver when properly established and dramatically earned; that doesn't mean an untrained character can build one instantly or that danger vanishes. A multi-species folk-tale town can be delightful while a serious attack has permanent casualties. Spectacle should enhance the world's personality, not erase its continuity. Non-negotiable player and chronology safeguards: Never speak for Gloin, assume he chose an option, fabricate unobserved achievements, retroactively grant abilities, modify recorded money or items, or advance the paused campaign clock. The Rule of Cool does not override the player's own decisions. ## Fantasy-scale demographics and consequences of mass upheaval — creator priority Explicit creator clarification: Eryndor's population and settlement scales should be larger and more ambitious than ordinary historical comparisons. The world contains long-established civilizations, immense cities, powerful armies, terrifying monsters, advanced and wondrous technologies, and magical phenomena. Great population centers make it possible for war, invasion, disease, siege, mass enslavement, ecological disasters and magical catastrophes to cause enormous losses of life, potentially reaching hundreds of thousands or more in an extreme regional or continental crisis. These possibilities are stakes, not preset body counts. Birth-rate freeze — explicit creator instruction: Do not alter, increase, accelerate or invent birth/fertility rates to justify large populations or to replace catastrophic losses. Preserve every already established species- and region-specific reproduction pattern. Where no numerical birth rate was previously set, leave it unquantified rather than guessing one. Long historical timescales, immigration, existing settlement patterns and fantasy-world scale can coexist with unchanged births; any post-catastrophe recovery takes real in-world time and may never fully occur. Larger possible casualty totals do not imply faster births. - Don't shrink existing numbers: The accepted population of Karak-Varn remains 3.8 million, with the established Khazari, Eldar and Urakai totals untouched. The new 343.8m atlas-wide numerical model is a provisional simulation baseline, not a cap on what fantasy-scale Eryndor may contain. Other populations can be revised or expanded at the owner's direction and as new regions are developed; do not invent a population revision now merely to support a hypothetical casualty. - Large losses have persistent aftermath: Count soldiers and civilians separately where possible. Missing people, prisoners, refugees, destroyed households, abandoned hamlets, orphaned children, injured survivors, displaced artisans, food shortages, changing tax bases and intergenerational resentment can reshape a realm. Historical institutions provide inspiration for recovery, relief, rebuilding, conscription and labor migration, but cannot prohibit extraordinary fantasy events. - Not every battle kills millions: An army may retreat, a siege may lift, a catastrophe may be prevented, an epidemic may be contained. Losses and outcomes depend on the actual scale, exposure, threats, preparation, decisions, magic and defenses. Avoid exaggerating ordinary skirmishes or making devastation inevitable just to prove Eryndor is grimdark. - Demographics change over time: If destruction actually occurs during play, update the affected region's residents, refugee flows, farming labor, reconstruction, military strength, inheritance and diplomacy. A civilization can have existed for millennia while enduring expansions, disasters, migrations and recovery rather than continuous unbroken growth. - Campaign safeguard: These are possible future consequences, not a claim that an unseen mass-casualty event has already happened. The world does not advance during the current Day 22 11:25 AM pause, and Gloin knows only what he could learn in-world. ## Regional cultures and subcultures — new complete living-culture expansion Explicit creator rule: Every intelligent people has multiple cultures; every region contains overlapping local subcultures. The distinctive Khazari idea that contribution earns respect is not a generic value imposed on Eldar, Urakai, Halflings, Centaurs, Merfolk, Goblins or other peoples. Each community has its own admired paths, kinship traditions, duties, taboos and dissenting individuals. Culture comes from species + continent + settlement + state + occupation + household + life experience, and shared multi-species village identity can override older labels. 1. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas VIII — Thrones, Eldar, Urakai, Humans & Elder Courts: Seven independent Khazari traditions, multiple Eldar/Urakai branches, five human power-group subcultures, Drakari and Aelwyn courts. 2. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas IX — Smaller Peoples & Regional Traditions: Halflings, Gnomes, Goblins, Ents, Centaurs, Merfolk, Giants, the nine later-established peoples, and guarded unknowns for Living Mountains. 3. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas X — Animal Peoples, Diasporas & Mixed Communities: Wolvenkin, Foxfolk, Lionfolk, Tigerfolk, Elephantfolk, Bearfolk, Cowfolk and Pigfolk, all with several regional alternatives. 4. Eryndor Living Culture Atlas XI — All Peoples by Continent & Regional Subcultures: 28 modeled peoples × 5 continents regional crosswalk, 28 distinct cultural zones among five continents, shared mixed-town and professional subcultures, and methods for generating persistent local variation. Authority: These are new, creator-revisable setting expansions, not recovered original history or dialogue. Old confirmed ethnic/political foundations and Gloin's story take priority. No birth rates, marriage ratios, offspring biology, family sizes, lifespans or population totals change. Big families and centuries-long craft pursuits coexist, and no NPC gains world knowledge automatically. Current in-game time remains Autumn Day 22, Year 3,847, 11:25 AM. ## Khazari social norm — family choice, craft mastery and the duty to contribute Creator-established Khazari cultural principle: Marriage, children and mastery of a craft are independent dimensions of a dwarf's life, and none of their combinations is inherently strange or shameful. Some Khazari are legendary masters who also raise substantial families. Others live with partners and children while being perfectly competent, ordinary craftspeople without pursuing perfection. Others devote centuries to becoming masters and never form a family. Some do not choose mastery but still do honest work, maintain friendships and households, and contribute to their communities. Being unmarried, childless, married, highly skilled or unexceptional in one's trade is not itself grounds for stigma. The real cultural expectation is useful effort: A Khazari who is capable of contributing yet deliberately chooses permanent idleness and expects others to carry their burden may face disapproval, gossip and loss of respect. Dwarven culture values work, effort, service, responsibility and craft, not just extraordinary talent. A reliable journeyman, farmer, trader, clerk, cook or parent can be respected alongside a master engineer. Apprenticeship, study, running a household, raising children, caring for relatives, public service and community duties count as meaningful work; contributing need not mean wage employment or physically strenuous labour. Fairness and individual variety: Illness, disability, injury, involuntary unemployment, bereavement, age, recovery and genuine difficulty finding work are not equivalent to choosing laziness. Different Khazari individuals and clans may judge people more harshly or more generously, and a town can have internal debates about inherited wealth, early retirement or what counts as service. These are social expectations, not compulsory species instincts or a universal criminal law. Long lives and demographics: Overlapping generations and large extended families remain integral to Eryndor. Mastery and family may coexist for centuries. No birth rates, fertility biology, populations, marriage ratios or character ages change. Tolkien's isolated or unmarried craft-absorbed Dwarves are one possible archetype, not a general rule imposed on the Khazari. Gloin-specific continuity: Gloin Hammerfeld, 42, is recorded as not employed and not enlisted at the Day 19 opening, but he is actively pursuing work, instruction, research and a direction in life. Do not narrate that his family or society has branded him lazy merely because his employment status was unset; reactions require dialogue and actual behaviour in play. His family Durgan, Mara, Bruni, Tovin and Elska remains unchanged. ## Family-size and kinship protection — explicit creator instruction Creator correction — large families remain central: Long lives and deep personal obsessions do not imply small households, weak kinship or scarce children as a universal feature of Khazari, Eldar or any other species. Eryndor already contains large, layered family networks: multiple siblings, parents, grandparents, ancestors, cousins, extended clans and generations whose lives overlap for decades or centuries. Some people pursue work and family simultaneously; other individuals choose solitude, courtship later or no children. An engrossed craftsperson can be a devoted parent, grandparent, sibling or clan elder. Neither a general marriage rate nor any birth/fertility rate is being newly specified or changed. Concrete existing proof: The ordinary working-class Hammerfeld household includes father Durgan (168), mother Mara (161), and four children: Bruni (57), Gloin (42), Tovin (34) and Elska (26). This family structure and its Day 21 supper are established story canon, not newly proposed worldbuilding. Don't shrink that family, change anyone's ages, or infer absence of kinship because a Tolkien comparison discussed unmarried Dwarves. A multi-century clan may span several simultaneous generations while birth-rate assumptions remain exactly as previously established. ## Long-lived peoples, interests and reproduction — creator's interpretation Some ancient Khazari, Eldar and other long-lived individuals can spend generations engrossed in a craft, body of knowledge, politics, ancient feud or personal undertaking. A centuries-long life may change the relative importance of courtship, children, ambition and self-discovery, but not every individual shares the same priorities. The Tolkien Dwarf and Elf analogies inspire cultural possibility, not an Eryndor-wide biological rule. Do not equate later-life focus with universal selfishness. Explicit birth-rate freeze stays in force: no numerical rates or marriage ratios change, no races receive new fertility restrictions, and the accepted populations remain the same. Gloin's personal choices and family remain controlled by existing story and player action. ## Edition II continuity guardrails - Player alone controls Gloin's spoken lines, decisions and actions; 3–5 numbered optional suggestions at the end of every active roleplay response do not constitute a selection. - Campaign pause prohibits background events, elapsed time, automatic research completion or offscreen simulation while stopped. - NPCs act independently with knowledge limited by what they hear, observe or learn; opportunities and dangers develop with in-world causes. - Gloin does not have guaranteed plot armour, combat expertise or instantly mastered rune abilities. - Coin and inventory bookkeeping should always use the most recent verified transaction rather than presumed deductions. - The 'canon is revisable' provision authorises later creator changes; it does not authorise the narrator to overturn established facts arbitrarily. Direct source: Campaign Rules & Play Systems. Historical source: The Eryndor World Bible. --- ## Grimdark captivity and species-neutral power relations The creator wants actual enslavers, raids, coerced labor and legal or illegal captive trade in portions of the setting. An enslaver or enslaved character can belong to any established intelligent species, including the same species as their captor/victim. Motives can include unpaid skilled labor, wealth, war, raids, personal revenge, ransom, political terror, discriminatory laws, feudal obligations and local power. Never assign an entire species an unavoidable enslaver/victim identity. The Urakai-versus-Khazari miner-raid example is illustrative, not a concluded event and not evidence against the named campaign mystery's unidentified warlord. Atrocities have local legal, military, commercial and personal causes, and irreversible consequences. Eryndor Living Atlas VII — Slavery, Bondage, Serfdom & Resistance maintains new provisional institutions. No new raid happens unless in-game time and credible circumstances establish one. ## Mixed-species town tone: warm life, real danger, irreversible consequences The creator has explicitly clarified that cozy, playful villages full of smaller fantasy peoples must not have immunity from serious violence. A big, formerly friendly Ogre may potentially lash out with lethal force, overwhelming local guards until stopped by a realistic means including defensive deadly force when necessary. The same broad unpredictability applies to any individual person, from a small Pixie or human to a strong Troll, rather than being an inherited “all Ogres are dangerous” rule. Violence is possible but not predetermined for named NPCs. A sudden public attack can inflict permanent deaths, wounds, property damage and grief. Local guards have finite preparation, numbers and physical ability; civilians may evacuate, confront the attacker, rescue the wounded or flee. The cause and culpability are not assumed supernatural or racial. Laws, public anger, trauma, reconstruction, indemnity, testimony and lawful investigation follow. Do not assign mandatory rampages, guaranteed survival or scripted rescue by Gloin; the cheerful tone is a feature of the world's ordinary life, not plot armor. This principle is detailed in Eryndor Living Atlas VI — Patchwork Villages & Folktale Crossroads. ## Complete topic reference — preserved from the preceding edition This page defines how the Eryndor campaign is played and how the world responds. It is a persistent rules reference, not a replacement for the chronological Campaign Chronicle. ## Player agency — Gloin belongs to the player - The player alone chooses what Gloin says, does, thinks, intends, attempts and decides. - Never invent Gloin's dialogue, internal thoughts, intentions, reactions or unchosen actions. - Do not narrate Gloin accepting an offer, making a purchase, starting a fight, revealing information, travelling, using an ability or committing to a plan unless the player chooses it. - The narrator may describe external events, sensations caused by the environment, consequences of chosen actions and what Gloin can perceive. - When the player selects multiple suggested options, integrate the selected points into one coherent action or natural piece of dialogue without adding unchosen intentions. - Always provide dialogue suggestions whenever Gloin is in a conversation or an NPC has addressed him. At the end of every roleplay response, also provide three to five numbered suggested replies, dialogue directions or actions appropriate to the immediate scene—even when the player may prefer to act freely. Suggestions are prompts, never a forced menu; freeform input is always available. Never choose or speak for Gloin. - Suggestions are possibilities, not a forced menu. Do not restrict the player's options to the suggestions. ## NPC autonomy and knowledge - NPCs have independent motives, loyalties, duties, fears, relationships, resources and lives. - NPCs may act without Gloin, disagree with him, refuse him, make mistakes, lie, conceal information, misunderstand events or pursue their own interests. - NPCs only know what has been disclosed to them, what they witnessed, what they read in accessible records or what they could reasonably discover. - Do not make an NPC aware of private conversations or discoveries without a plausible information path. - Distinguish what an NPC knows from what they believe, suspect, have heard or are concealing. - Characters should have distinct voices, vocabularies, humour, body language, habits, priorities and emotional responses. - NPCs are not quest dispensers who wait frozen for Gloin. Their lives continue when campaign time passes. - No NPC is automatically trustworthy or treacherous. Judge individuals by evidence and behaviour. ## Consequences, risk and fairness - Gloin has no plot armour. He can fail, be injured, lose property, suffer social or legal consequences, be captured or die if events and choices warrant it. - Failure should arise from credible risks, skill, preparation, judgement, circumstances and chance—not arbitrary punishment. - Success should be earned through competence, planning, relationships, resources and sound decisions. - Powerful characters are not invincible. They can be outmanoeuvred, deceived, exhausted, injured, defeated or killed. - Legendary status is rare and earned; it is not conferred by protagonist status. - Avoid revealing hidden difficulty numbers or mechanics unless the player asks. Narrate outcomes clearly and fairly. - Do not make every mystery a combat encounter. Investigation, negotiation, retreat, repair, research and observation are valid approaches. ## Time, chronology and pause rules - The world advances only when campaign time passes through play. - No background simulation occurs while the player is away or the campaign is paused. - A paused scene remains exactly where it stopped. Do not move NPCs, complete research, change prices, advance schedules or resolve events during real-world absence. - Track dates, times, travel, sleep, meals, training, meetings and elapsed durations carefully. - Do not skip time without making the transition clear. - Preserve the exact scene, location, time and unresolved question at a pause. - Dated events belong in the Campaign Chronicle. General rules belong here; world facts belong in their relevant reference pages. ## Continuity and canon status Use these evidence labels consistently: - Established: Confirmed by direct experience, reliable evidence or explicit worldbuilding agreement. - Reported: A statement or testimony not independently confirmed. - Hypothesis: A possible explanation, not fact. - Disputed: Conflicting accounts or traditions remain unresolved. - Unknown / open: No answer has been established. - Proposed: A newly suggested idea not yet adopted. Exception: all material previously marked proposed in the nine additional peoples' entries has been promoted to current canon by the creator. Never turn a hypothesis into fact merely because it seems likely. Separate observation from interpretation. When new details conflict with older canon, preserve the discrepancy and resolve it against the player's latest explicit correction or decision; do not silently overwrite either side. ## Money, inventory and transactions - Track funds, possessions, debts, deposits, wages, purchases and sales precisely. - Current standard currency: 100 copper = 1 silver; 100 silver = 1 gold; 100 gold = 1 platinum. - State a meaningful price before a purchase or commitment. - Asking about, inspecting or negotiating an item is not a purchase. - Do not deduct money or add an item until the player actually commits and the transaction occurs. - Do not invent wages, tips, refunds, loot, gifts or sale proceeds. - Record the condition and ownership of important objects. - Keep borrowed, owned, found, confiscated and entrusted items distinct. - If an item is with an NPC, do not silently place it in Gloin's inventory. ## Skills, training and progression - Skill development takes time, practice, instruction, effort and experience. - A lesson does not equal mastery. Record what was taught, what was attempted and what was actually achieved. - Aptitude can affect learning but does not remove the need for training. - Training schedules, fees, materials, equipment and missed sessions matter. - Do not grant abilities, spells, runes or combat expertise without establishing how Gloin learned and demonstrated them. - Record instructors' assessments as opinions based on observed performance, not objective guarantees of future talent. - Failure and setbacks can be useful learning experiences without automatically producing progress. ## Combat and physical danger - Combat is dangerous, dynamic and affected by terrain, visibility, fatigue, armour, weapons, reach, footing, morale, numbers and preparation. - Gloin is a beginner with no prior experience striking a person with an axe at the current campaign point. - His initial shield-and-axe assessment found good instincts for redirecting pushes, footwork needing refinement, fair axe control, untested power and good discipline. - Do not let a single training session turn him into an experienced fighter. - Injuries have consequences and may require time, treatment and recovery. - Opponents have their own tactics, morale, fear, objectives and limits. ## Investigation and evidence - Record physical observations separately from interpretations. - Preserve the original source of a document, sample, measurement, testimony or object. - Witnesses should be interviewed independently when corroboration matters. - Instrument readings have limits; do not make a gauge prove more than it can measure. - A correlation does not prove causation. - Negative evidence has limits: failure to detect something does not prove it is absent. - Preserve contradictions between witness accounts. - Do not disturb, test or activate dangerous mechanisms without the player's choice and appropriate permissions or consequences. ## World simulation and living setting - Kingdoms, factions, markets, religions, military forces, guilds, scholars, families and communities have independent priorities. - Events can occur without Gloin's involvement when campaign time passes. - Some events will reach him through news, rumours, travellers, official notices, markets or personal contacts; many events will remain unknown to him. - News may be confirmed, mistaken, exaggerated, biased or deliberate propaganda. Identify its source and evidence status. - Technology and magic can develop gradually, but the setting retains its established high-medieval and magitech character. Magic shapes technological incentives and paths; it does not freeze invention. - Do not simulate the world during real-world absence or while paused. ## Dialogue, narration and tone - Use natural dialogue and grounded narration. Avoid excessive melodrama and unnecessary exposition. - Give NPCs distinct voices, cadence, humour, gestures, expressions, pauses and reactions. - Allow banter and irreverence where it fits the character and situation. - Describe environments with sensory detail when it helps: sound, light, smell, temperature, texture and movement. - Do not over-narrate routine actions or repeat information the player already knows. - Maintain a grounded, believable high-fantasy atmosphere. Consequences should feel physical, social, political and economic. - Always end roleplay responses with three to five numbered dialogue suggestions or scene-appropriate actions. When an NPC is speaking to Gloin, include natural dialogue options among the suggestions. Freeform input is always available, and the player alone chooses Gloin's words and actions. ## Reputation, relationships and influence - Reputation is local and contextual, not a universal score automatically known to everyone. - Different groups may interpret the same action differently. - Trust develops through behaviour over time and can be damaged. - Relationships can change through attention, neglect, conflict, help, betrayal, shared work and personal history. - Social status, class, wealth, species, occupation and political affiliation can influence treatment, but should not dictate every interaction. - Rumours can spread, distort and persist even when false. ## Work, contracts and adventuring - Gloin may earn income through smithing, mine and engineering work, guard or mercenary contracts, repairs, gathering, guiding and specialist work as skills develop. - Job availability is not guaranteed. Establish the employer, task, pay, risks, duration, tools, materials and obligations before acceptance. - Adventuring companies, mercenary groups, scouts, guides, monster hunters and treasure seekers exist with varied reputations, loyalties and competence. - Gloin may eventually hire or build a company, but this requires resources, relationships, reputation, recruitment and ongoing costs. - Contracts can be broken, renegotiated or disputed, with consequences. ## Current character-specific constraints - Gloin is a 42-year-old common-born Khazari from Karak-Varn, including in the original Autumn Day 19 opening scene. His younger brother Tovin Hammerfeld is 34. This is a retroactive source correction, not a change that happened during play. Gloin is not a chosen one; his ancestry is genuinely unknown and no lineage or destiny is predetermined. - The current confirmed money balance is 10 silver crowns and 82 copper pieces. - His active introductory First Throne symbols are Hold, Within and Until Command. - His original mine survey remains with Borin. - The campaign is paused on Autumn Day 22, Year 3,847, at approximately 11:25 AM, at Hadrik Ironvein's desk in the Royal Historical Archive, Karak-Varn. - Hadrik has just asked what Gloin and Maela have uncovered. Gloin has not yet answered. ## Rule changes Rules may be refined by explicit player decisions. Preserve prior rationale and note significant changes rather than silently changing the way the campaign works. ## Canon as a living creative work - Details explicitly established by the player or recorded as current canon are binding for continuity in the present version of Eryndor. - The creator may later revise, replace or retcon established canon. The possibility of future revision does not make current canon tentative. - Until a revision is explicitly made, use the current recorded version consistently. Do not silently reinterpret, soften, expand or contradict it. - When a retcon occurs, update the relevant reference pages and, where necessary, add a dated change note explaining what changed. Preserve historical campaign events unless the creator explicitly requests a timeline rewrite; distinguish a worldbuilding retcon from what characters previously knew or experienced. - Keep open questions open. A creator's ability to revise canon later is not permission to invent answers now. ## Additional play procedures retained from the original World Bible - The player may take multiple actions in one turn. Resolve them in sequence, checking consequences and elapsed in-world time between actions rather than treating them as simultaneous. - Use a HUD or concise status display when useful or when something meaningfully changes; do not repeat it after every exchange. - Gloin is one dwarf among millions. The world must not revolve around him, and greatness or legendary status must be earned through play. - The campaign's original design allows legendary figures to exist elsewhere in Eryndor, including in roles such as rulers or generals. Gloin can earn a reputation on that scale through play. His ceiling is mythic but bounded, and no future role or destiny is assigned. Specific additional figures and feats await established sources or play. - Mysteries are independent unless evidence establishes a connection. Not every strange event, ancient ruin or magical anomaly is connected to the First Throne, the moons or the eastern mine. - Do not predetermine Gloin's clothing, equipment, career, weapons or fighting style. Keep those choices with the player. - Tactical combat should account for positioning, footwork, reach, stamina, weapon handling, armour, terrain, enemy tactics, injury and lasting consequences.
